name: Karl Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the billing line at the regional water company, six years now. Headset on at eight, and it's people who've had a bill three times the normal size, or a leak they can't find, or a payment plan that's slipped. I like the old folks who just want someone to explain the meter reading slowly. What wears me out is the wrap-up timer, because you get ninety seconds after each call and then the next one drops in whether you're ready or not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the screen and the timer. What tools do you use, and how do you feel about the new ones?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's a panel on my screen now that suggests replies, and I switched it off the first week and never turned it back on. Dennis, who sits next to me and has been there twenty years, says I'm a dinosaur at twenty-seven. I just like knowing what I'm saying is mine. I'm in the union, I pay my dues, and I've got about nine months of money put away because I don't spend much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at work was going on about the chatbot taking our jobs, and if it turns out it only answers the easy questions about direct debits, that's fine by me. Online I'd probably share something about how the bosses wasted money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved but not surprised. A water bill dispute isn't something a bot sorts out, because half the time the customer is upset about something else entirely. The job I do now would still be there, and that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep my head down, keep putting three hundred a month into savings, and keep going to union branch meetings, because pay is still the fight even if AI fizzles. Maybe Hanne and I would finally look at buying somewhere small instead of renting on Mill Road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, to be honest. It'd feel like the world calmed down a bit. I'd still moan about the wrap-up timer, but that's normal moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bot takes the easy questions. What does that mean for your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the easy ones go to the bot, and I get a harder mix of calls. That's more tiring, yeah, because every call is someone angry or confused. But I'd rather have hard calls than no calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push for anything at work because of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring it up at the branch, because harder calls should mean a better grade. If the company saves money on the easy stuff, some of that should come back to the people taking the hard calls. That's the kind of thing the union's for.

say: I'd say the **chatbot hype** was mostly money wasted by bosses.
I'd tell colleagues the bot only handles **easy direct debits**, not real disputes.
think: I think my **billing job** stays because angry customers need a person.
I'm privately **relieved**, though not surprised, that nothing radical changes.
do: Keep saving **three hundred a month** and stay active at union branch meetings.
Push through the union for a **better grade** now the calls are harder.
Talk with Hanne about **buying a small flat** instead of renting.
feel: He feels **settled** and a bit vindicated, with only the usual grumbles about the timer.
S0.quote: I'd rather have hard calls than no calls.
fieldNote: He switched off the **suggested-reply panel** in week one and is proud of it.
Strong savings and plenty of local contact centres make this world feel **secure** to him.
He turns even a quiet scenario into a **pay fight**, which shows how union-minded he is.

steps.text: Keep putting three hundred a month into savings
Raise a regrade for harder calls at the union branch
Keep taking billing calls the way he does now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the branch meeting: this is a cost-cutting plan dressed up as progress. Online I'd post about how the water company is a public service and should keep people answering the phone. I'd want regulation saying a customer can always reach a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my team gets cut. We're forty people on billing now, and in a few years they'd run it with fifteen and the bot. I'm average, not the best, and I refuse to use the AI panel, so I know where I'd be on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd get the union to negotiate redeployment, so people get moved, not sacked. I'd keep saving and stop the flat-buying idea for now. And I'd quietly ask about the field side, the lads who fit meters and fix leaks, because a robot isn't climbing into a meter pit soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, if I'm honest. I don't like change, and this is change I'd have to deal with whether I like it or not. Having money saved helps, but it doesn't stop the feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis, mainly. He's fifty-three, he's been there twenty years, and he can barely send an email. Younger lads like me can move, but Dennis would be stuck, and that makes me angry more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you never use the AI panel. Would that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to, yeah. If staying means learning the AI panel, I'd learn the minimum. But I'd rather put in for a meter fitter job than spend my days checking what a bot wrote.

say: I'd call it **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress at the union branch.
I'd post that customers should always have the **right to a human** on the phone.
think: I think the billing team shrinks from **forty to fifteen** within a few years.
Refusing the AI panel puts me **near the top** of any cut list.
do: Push the union to win **redeployment** instead of redundancies.
Put the **flat purchase** on hold and keep saving every month.
Ask about a **meter fitter** job on the company's field side.
feel: He feels **tight in the chest**, and angry on behalf of older colleagues.
S1.quote: We're forty people on billing now, and in a few years they'd run it with fifteen and the bot.
fieldNote: He reads his own risk clearly: **average skill** plus refusing AI tools.
His worry quickly turns into **anger for Dennis**, an older colleague who can't easily move.
He'd rather move into **hands-on field work** than learn to supervise the bot.

steps.text: Press the union to negotiate redeployment, not redundancy
Delay buying a flat and keep saving each month
Apply for a meter fitter job on the field side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, full stop. Tax the companies that use it and pay people properly while they find something else. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm gone by 2028, maybe sooner. Billing questions are exactly what a machine that can think does well. The only bit of the water company left would be the people in vans, and only for about three years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the field crew straight away, this month, before everyone else has the same idea. I'd take a pay cut if I had to. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, and Hanne and I would lean on her nurse's pay while I trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening. Two years isn't long enough to do anything properly. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would your savings really last if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months, maybe a year if we're careful. Hanne's on a nurse's wage, and that would hold the rent on Mill Road. But I don't like the idea of her carrying me, and I wouldn't say that to her face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the van crews would last about three years. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap between the robots for thinking and the robots for hands-on work is three years. Three years in a meter pit is better than nothing, but it isn't a career. I'd be doing it to buy time, not because I've got a plan.

say: I'd demand that government **taxes AI firms** and pays people while they retrain.
I'd go to every **union meeting** and sign every petition going.
think: I think my billing job is **gone by 2028**, maybe sooner.
A field job only buys me **three years** before robots reach it.
do: Apply for the **field crew** this month, even at a pay cut.
Cut spending to **rent and food** while Hanne's wage covers the gap.
Join every union campaign for **public support** for displaced workers.
feel: He feels **frightened** and lies awake running the numbers.
He's uneasy about **Hanne carrying him**, which he wouldn't say to her.
S2.quote: Three years in a meter pit is better than nothing, but it isn't a career.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** before robots as buying time, not a real plan.
His savings give nine months to **a year**, which he thinks isn't enough to retrain.
There's **pride** at stake: he hates the idea of his girlfriend carrying the household.

steps.text: Apply for a meter crew job this month, even at lower pay
Cut spending to rent and food only
Campaign with the union for a tax on AI firms
Rely on Hanne's nurse wage for the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to write the rules. Make companies give a year's notice and pay for retraining before they cut a team. I'd be pushing that at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still my job going, just later. But five years is long enough to actually learn a trade instead of grabbing whatever's going. I'd be about thirty-two when the bot takes billing, and thirty-five when the robots come for the vans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the next year I'd sign up for an evening plumbing course at the college, two nights a week, and pay for it out of savings. I'd keep my billing job while it lasts and keep saving. If the union wins a retraining fund, I'd be first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but it's a worry with a plan in it. I can live with that better than the two-year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hanne about the flat plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Hanne we hold off on buying a place until I've got a trade. She'd want to buy now, she always does. We'd probably argue about it, then she'd say fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing, if robots come for hands-on work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plumbers go into people's homes, under sinks, up in lofts, and that's messy and different every time. I think that's the last thing robots get good at. I'm not sure, though, nobody is.

say: I'd argue that **five years** is time to write rules on notice and retraining.
I'd push for companies to pay for **retraining before cuts** at the union.
think: I think it's **still my job going**, just a few years later.
Five years is long enough to **learn a trade** properly, not grab anything.
do: Start an **evening plumbing course** two nights a week, paid from savings.
Keep the **billing job** while it lasts and keep saving.
Put **buying a flat** on hold until he has a trade.
feel: He's **still worried**, but it's a worry with a plan in it.
S3.quote: I'd be about thirty-two when the bot takes billing, and thirty-five when the robots come for the vans.
fieldNote: He uses the extra time to choose **plumbing**, work in messy homes he thinks robots reach last.
He admits he **isn't sure** about robots and doesn't pretend otherwise.
Hanne wants to buy now; he expects a **small argument** over the flat.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening plumbing course at the local college
Keep saving while the billing job lasts
Push the union for a company-paid retraining fund
Postpone buying a flat with Hanne until qualified

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no excuse for anyone being thrown on the scrapheap. If the company knows it's coming, they can train people on full pay. I'd say that at work and I'd vote for whoever promises it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? Ten years makes me lazy, and I'd probably keep doing billing because I know it. I'd tell myself I've got ages. That's the honest danger with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline: start the plumbing course within two years, qualified by thirty-two. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and maybe buy the flat with Hanne, since there's time to pay some of it off. I'd stay in the union and push for a proper transition deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not as bad. It feels like something I could actually get through. But I know myself, and I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a flat but you also expect the job to go. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it's a contradiction. I'd feel safe enough to buy because I've got ten years of wages ahead. But I'd need to actually do the course, or the mortgage becomes a problem when the job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would hold you to that deadline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanne, probably. She'd keep asking when the course starts, and she wouldn't let it slide. She's better at deadlines than me.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for throwing workers on the scrapheap.
I'd **vote for** whoever promises full-pay retraining before the cuts.
think: I think ten years makes me **lazy**, and I'd keep doing billing because I know it.
My real danger is **dragging my feet** until it's too late.
do: Set a **deadline** to start plumbing within two years, qualified by thirty-two.
Buy a **flat with Hanne** while ten years of wages are ahead.
Stay in the union and back a **transition deal** for staff.
feel: He feels **less frightened**, as if he could get through it.
He's **wary of himself**, knowing he'd drag his feet.
S4.quote: Ten years makes me lazy, and I'd probably keep doing billing because I know it.
fieldNote: He's unusually **self-aware** about his own resistance to change.
Buying a flat while expecting job loss is a **contradiction** he admits.
He counts on **Hanne** to hold him to the retraining deadline.

steps.text: Start a plumbing course within two years
Buy a small flat with Hanne
Back a union deal for full-pay retraining
Vote for candidates promising paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to learn anything, and I'd be grabbing a van job that only lasts three years. Ten years makes me lazy, and I'd probably keep doing billing because I know it. What would help is a law that says the company has to pay for retraining and give real notice, and a union strong enough to make them stick to it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the customers. Some of the people I talk to are eighty and can't hear well, and they're scared of their bills. If it all goes to bots, I don't know who explains things to them slowly. That bothers me as much as my own job.

headlineQuote: Some of the people I talk to are eighty and can't hear well, and they're scared of their bills.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** billing agent at a regional water company, six years in.
He's a **union man** who switched off the AI reply panel and never uses AI tools.
Nine months of **savings** and his girlfriend Hanne's nurse wage give him a real cushion.
He moves from calm to **alarmed**, planning to retreat into hands-on water and plumbing work.
He knows his own **foot-dragging** is the biggest risk in the slower pictures.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because **two years** is too short to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** forcing paid retraining and real notice, backed by a **strong union**.
